title: Clinical and Economic Impact of Inotersen for the Treatment of Hereditary Transthyretin Amyloidosis (ATTRv) in Adults: A Systematic Review
content: Background and objectives. Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv) is a rare, progressive disease caused by deposition of transthyretin-derived amyloid fibrils. Inotersen, an antisense oligonucleotide that inhibits hepatic transthyretin production, is approved by the FDA and EMA but is not fully implemented in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). We systematically reviewed the evidence on the efficacy, safety and economic impact of inotersen in adults with ATTRv, jointly synthesizing clinical and economic evidence with particular attention to its transferability to LMICs, where treatment access remains limited.Methods. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, CENTRAL and SciELO for efficacy and safety evidence, and EconLit, NHS-EED and the CEA Registry (in addition to the clinical databases) for economic evidence (July–August 2025), without language or date restrictions. We followed PRISMA guidelines for reporting our findings. We included randomized controlled trials and economic evaluations with or without economic modelling. Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently, with a senior reviewer for solving discrepancies. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2.0 (randomized evidence), ROBINS-I for open-label studies and the Philips and Drummond checklists for economic studies. We synthesised the information retrieved without a meta-analysis.Results. One pivotal trial (NEURO-TTR), reported across five publications including a 170-week open-label extension, and six economic evaluations were included. Inotersen improved neuropathy and quality-of-life outcomes (e.g., mNIS+7 difference −19.7; 95% CI −26.4 to −13.0; Norfolk QoL-DN −11.7; 95% CI −18.3 to −5.1), but serious adverse events — including grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia — were more frequent with inotersen. All economic evaluations adopted a payer perspective; cost-effectiveness ratios were well above conventional thresholds (e.g., ICUR CA$1,322,377/QALY [CADTH reanalysis]; £150,636/QALY [NICE]; €382,984/QALY [NCPE]). Only one study came from a middle-income country (a Mexican budget-impact analysis; US$2.3 million/year, 0.036% of the national health budget) and reported no cost-effectiveness estimate. Risk of bias was moderate for the NEURO-TTR trial and critical for the open-label extension.Conclusions. The evidence favoured inotersen for efficacy and safety in the short term, although long-term evidence is uncertain. Economic studies indicate that inotersen is not cost-effective at current market prices. Evaluation frameworks for rare and orphan diseases are needed to inform the introduction of these therapies where no treatment is currently available, particularly in LMICs.
